analysis.one_liner: Slashes the tax on U.S. corporations' foreign profits brought back home to 5%, permanently.
analysis.headline: The Rebuilding America Act died without a vote: referred to the Senate Finance Committee in November 2011 and never scheduled for any action before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let U.S. companies bring profits they hold overseas back to the United States while paying only a 5% tax instead of the standard 35% corporate rate, and it would make that low rate a permanent option rather than a one-time deal. Companies hold an estimated $2.3 trillion in foreign accounts that would become eligible. Supporters said the money would fund domestic investment and jobs; critics of such holidays point out that companies could simply keep profits offshore and shuttle them back at the low rate whenever they choose, and the Treasury would collect far less on those profits.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. multinational corporations with large piles of overseas profits, especially cash-rich technology and pharmaceutical companies. They would cut their tax bill on repatriated foreign earnings from 35% to 5%, permanently, and could time repatriations to maximize the benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the tax rate on foreign earnings that U.S. corporations reinvest in the United States from 35% to 5% by allowing a deduction equal to 85.7% of the repatriated amount.
Makes the low repatriation rate permanent: any company could elect it for any tax year, covering both current and accumulated foreign earnings, rather than a one-time window as in the 2004 holiday.
The bill's findings state that U.S. multinationals hold an estimated $2.3 trillion in foreign accounts and argues high taxes keep them from investing that money domestically.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and the Treasury, which would collect 5 cents instead of 35 cents on each dollar of repatriated foreign profit, permanently. If the revenue gap were not closed elsewhere, it would be made up through deficits, future taxes, or cuts to public programs.

drawbacks.text: The permanent 5% rate would cut federal revenue on foreign profits by seven-eighths, and because the election never expires, companies could plan around it indefinitely rather than making a one-time surge of investment.

The bill rewards the structure it is meant to fix: companies that kept profits offshore to avoid U.S. tax would get the biggest windfall, and a permanent low rate could encourage more profit-shifting abroad.

A one-time repatriation holiday in 2004 was widely reported to have sent most of the money to shareholders through buybacks and dividends rather than to new jobs and investment; making the incentive permanent would extend that pattern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The argument for the bill is that $2.3 trillion sitting offshore would come home and be invested. The cost is that the federal government would permanently collect 5% instead of 35% on those profits, the companies that avoided U.S. tax the most aggressively would gain the most, and the permanent election gives companies a standing tool to time repatriations rather than a one-time stimulus. On balance, the design directs most of the benefit to the companies and their shareholders, with the public absorbing the revenue loss.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on November 9, 2011 with five Republican cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; that is the last action of any kind in the record.
No markup, hearing, vote, or floor action ever occurred before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Treasury kept the standard 35% tax on repatriated foreign profits, and multinationals holding an estimated $2.3 trillion offshore did not receive the permanent 5% rate. Companies that had lobbied for a repatriation holiday gained nothing from this attempt.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on November 9, 2011.

for.name: 5 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Crapo, DeMint, Paul, Risch, Blunt)

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup, hearing, or vote after it was referred on November 9, 2011; no committee action appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All six senators behind the bill were Republicans, no Democrat cosponsored it, and no vote was ever held, so the only recorded support was one-sided.

industries.note: They would pay 5% instead of 35% on foreign profits brought home, permanently, and could elect the rate in any year. Their gain would come directly out of federal revenue that otherwise funds public spending.
These industries hold the largest overseas cash piles, so they would capture the largest share of the tax savings. The bill's own findings put total offshore holdings at an estimated $2.3 trillion.
